toolUseResult.originalFile:
---
title: Capabilities
description: What your deployment advertises to clients, what each capability means, and how you control it.
---

Custos tells clients what it can do. `com.atproto.server.describeServer` — the
public, unauthenticated endpoint every AT Protocol client already calls — carries
an extra `custos` object alongside the standard fields:

```json
{
  "did": "did:web:pds.example.com",
  "availableUserDomains": ["example.com"],
  "inviteCodeRequired": true,
  "phoneVerificationRequired": false,
  "custos": {
    "version": "0.8.1",
    "capabilities": ["sovereignSessions", "walletConsent", "didWebHosting"]
  }
}
```

A client reads `capabilities` and enables the matching features. Obsign, for
example, only offers to create a brand-new identity on a server that advertises
`createCeremony`, and only offers escrow-assisted recovery where `escrow` is
advertised — instead of calling the endpoint and interpreting the failure.

Two properties follow from this being a **list of named capabilities rather than
an "is this Custos?" flag**. First, your deployment is described by what it
actually offers: a Custos server running without a master key advertises fewer
capabilities, and clients adapt rather than break. Second, a server that sends no
`custos` object at all — the reference PDS, rsky-pds, millipds — simply has none
of these, and a well-behaved client falls back to standard AT Protocol behaviour.
Nothing here is required of anyone; the extension is additive, and clients that
do not know the field ignore it.

The complete, generated list lives in the
[capability reference](/operator/reference/capabilities/). This page explains what
each capability means for you and how to switch it on.

## Identifying your server

`GET /xrpc/_health` reports a self-identifying version string rather than a bare
number:

```json
{ "version": "custos v0.8.1", "db": "ok" }
```

This is the shape third-party AT Protocol diagnostic tooling reads to fingerprint
an implementation (millipds reports `millipds v…` the same way; the reference PDS
returns a bare commit hash that names no software). It is also what Obsign pings
when you point it at a server. Nothing in it is sensitive: it names software and
version, which any protocol-level probe can already infer.

## The capabilities

Each heading below is the literal name that appears in `custos.capabilities`.

### `createCeremony`

Custos-native identity creation: mobile signup, per-account repo signing key
issuance, and the client-authored `did:plc` genesis ceremony in which the user's
device key is written into the DID's rotation keys from the very first operation.
This is the only way an identity is born already sovereign — the standard
`createAccount` lexicon never lets a client author its own genesis rotation keys.

Without it, a wallet steers users to *import* an existing identity instead, and
the claim ceremony takes sovereign custody of an identity hosted anywhere.

**Controlled by:** `signing_key_master_key`. The ceremony issues each account a
repo signing key and stores it encrypted under the master key, so a deployment
with no `EZPDS_SIGNING_KEY_MASTER_KEY` cannot perform it and does not advertise
it. There is no separate switch: configure a master key (as any real deployment
should — see [Configuration](/operator/configuration/)) and the capability
appears.

### `escrow`

Custos holds one share of the account's 2-of-3 Shamir recovery split — encrypted,
and useless on its own — and releases it through the recovery gate: an emailed
one-time code, then a cancellable delay window during which the account holder is
notified and can abort. This is what makes recovery possible for a user who has
lost their device but still holds one share.

Without it, the wallet's recovery story is entirely self-held: the user keeps
both remaining shares themselves, and no server is involved in recovery at all.

**Controlled by:** `signing_key_master_key`. The stored share envelope is
encrypted under the master key, so a deployment without one cannot accept a
deposit or perform a release, and does not advertise the capability. The delay
window itself is tuned separately with `recovery.release_delay_secs`
(`EZPDS_RECOVERY_RELEASE_DELAY_SECS`, default 24 hours) — that changes how a
release behaves, not whether escrow is offered.

### `sovereignSessions`

Passwordless full-access sessions. Instead of a password, the client signs a
fresh, timestamped, nonce-bound proof with a key that is already in the
identity's current PLC rotation keys, and Custos verifies it against
plc.directory — never against a cached document. The account holder's device key
*is* the credential, so an account can have no password at all.

Everything that needs a full-access session rides on this: app passwords,
changing a handle, removing an identity, restoring media from a backup.

**Controlled by:** always. This is inherent to running Custos and has no operator
switch. It grants Custos no additional power over an identity — any current
rotation key qualifies, and rotation keys are the account holder's to control.

### `agents`

The [auth.md](https://github.com/workos/auth.md) agent surface: an AI agent or
automation registers with the server, the account holder confirms the claim from
their wallet (reading the exact scopes first), and the agent then exchanges its
assertion for narrowly-scoped, revocable, audited access tokens. Agent tokens can
never manage agents — including themselves — and every registration is revocable
from the wallet or by the identity provider.

**Controlled by:** `agent_auth.service_auth_enabled`,
`agent_auth.anonymous_enabled`, `agent_auth.trusted_issuers`. These are the three
ways an agent can register, and **all three are off or empty by default** — an
untouched deployment does not offer agents at all. Enable whichever registration
flows you want (`EZPDS_AGENT_AUTH_SERVICE_AUTH_ENABLED`,
`EZPDS_AGENT_AUTH_ANONYMOUS_ENABLED`, or a configured `[[agent_auth.trusted_issuers]]`
entry) and the capability appears. What a claimed agent may then do is bounded
separately by `agent_auth.granted_scopes`; narrowing it narrows every assertion
minted afterwards.

### `walletConsent`

An OAuth authorization can be approved in the identity wallet with a
device-key-signed decision, rather than by typing a password into a browser
consent page. The signed envelope binds the request, the client, the decision,
and the exact scope set, so an approval cannot be replayed onto a different
request, flipped from a denial, or widened after the fact.

**Controlled by:** always. This is inherent to running Custos and has no operator
switch. Password-based browser consent continues to work for accounts that have a
password; the wallet path is an additional, stronger route to the same grant.

### `didWebHosting`

Custos serves an opted-in account's `did:web` document at the account's own
domain (`/.well-known/did.json`) and emits an identity event so relays re-resolve
after an edit.

Hosting is opt-in **per account**, never automatic, and only ever for a domain
the user controls: moving the document onto Custos trades away some of the
independence a self-hosted document gives an identity, so it is the account
holder's decision. Exit is a DNS repoint away.

**Controlled by:** always. The server-side capability is inherent to running
Custos and has no operator switch; whether any given account uses it is that
account holder's choice.

### `waitlist`

A public interest-signup waitlist for a pre-launch deployment: an unauthenticated
`POST /waitlist` accepting an email address plus an optional atproto handle, meant
to be posted to directly from a marketing page on another origin (the endpoint is
CORS-open and carries no credentials). Signups are idempotent per email — a repeat
returns the same success and never discloses whether an address was already on the
list — and the handle is syntax-checked but deliberately never resolved, so the
endpoint has no outbound-request surface. The operator reads the list back with
`GET /v1/admin/waitlist` (newest first, with a total), which keeps working even
after the public endpoint is switched off again.

**Controlled by:** `waitlist.enabled`. Off by default — an instance that isn't
running a launch funnel should not carry a public write endpoint it never asked
for. Enable it with `[waitlist] enabled = true` (`EZPDS_WAITLIST_ENABLED`) and the
capability appears; the per-IP signup rate cap is `rate_limit.waitlist_per_5min`
(`EZPDS_RATE_LIMIT_WAITLIST_PER_5MIN`, default 30).

## Keeping this page honest

The capability table in the server source
(`crates/pds/src/capabilities.rs`) is the single source of truth: it holds each
capability's wire name, the configuration that gates it, and the predicate the
server actually evaluates. The
[capability reference](/operator/reference/capabilities/) is generated from it,
and a CI gate (`just capability-docs-check`) fails the build if a capability is
added, renamed, or re-gated without this page being updated in the same change.
If a "Controlled by" line above disagrees with your server's behaviour, that is a
bug, not a documentation lag — please report it.

=== sample ===
Groundwork for encrypted push notifications: Custos gained the sealing layer that will let a self-hosted instance send notifications through a relay it does not have to trust. Payloads are sealed to a per-device key with HPKE (RFC 9180, DHKEM-P256 + AES-256-GCM, authenticated mode), so a relay operator and Apple both see only opaque bytes and neither can forge a notification your device will accept. Payloads are also padded up to one of three fixed sizes: that does not hide length outright, but it reduces what length can reveal from a per-notification fingerprint to which of three buckets a notification fell into. Nothing is enabled by this change on its own; the relay, the registration flow, and the on-device decryption arrive in the phases that follow.

3	// Password hashing (argon2id) and verification. No I/O, no database, no state.
4	
5	use argon2::{

7	    Argon2, PasswordHash, PasswordHasher, PasswordVerifier,
8	};

10	use common::{ApiError, ErrorCode};
11	
12	/// Outcome of verifying a password against a stored hash.
13	///
14	/// Callers must handle `CorruptHash` separately from `WrongPassword`:
15	/// - `WrongPassword` → increment rate-limit counter, return 401
16	/// - `CorruptHash`   → log with identifier, return 500, do NOT increment counter
17	pub(crate) enum VerifyResult {
18	    /// Password is correct.
19	    Ok,
20	    /// Password is wrong (argon2 computed but didn't match).
21	    WrongPassword,
22	    /// The stored hash is not a valid PHC string — possible DB corruption.
23	    CorruptHash,
24	}
25	
26	/// A valid argon2id PHC string used as dummy input for timing equalization when a
27	/// login identifier is not found. This never matches any real user's password — its
28	/// only purpose is to ensure that the "identifier not found" path spends the same
29	/// wall-clock time as the "wrong password" path, preventing account-enumeration via
30	/// timing side-channels.
31	///
32	/// Parameters match `Argon2::default()` (argon2id v19, m=19456, t=2, p=1). The salt
33	/// and hash are 16 and 32 bytes of zeros respectively, expressed as base64 without
34	/// padding (standard alphabet). Using a compile-time constant avoids the panic risk
35	/// of the `OnceLock` + `unwrap` pattern.
36	pub(crate) const TIMING_DUMMY_HASH: &str =
37	    "$argon2id$v=19$m=19456,t=2,p=1$AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA$AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA";
38	
39	/// Hash `password` with argon2id and return the PHC string.
40	///
41	/// Uses `Argon2::default()` (argon2id, m=19456 KiB ≈19 MiB, t=2, p=1) with a freshly
42	/// generated random salt. The PHC string embeds the algorithm, parameters, salt, and
43	/// hash — everything `verify_password` needs for later verification.
44	pub(crate) fn hash_password(password: &str) -> Result<String, ApiError> {
45	    let salt = SaltString::generate(&mut OsRng);
46	    Argon2::default()
47	        .hash_password(password.as_bytes(), &salt)
48	        .map(|h| h.to_string())
49	        .map_err(|e| {
50	            tracing::error!(error = %e, "argon2id hashing failed");
51	            ApiError::new(ErrorCode::InternalError, "failed to process password")
52	        })
53	}
54	
55	/// What a newly created account's `accounts.password_hash` column becomes — resolved from the
56	/// request shape and the operator's policy before any state is written.
57	pub(crate) enum PasswordDisposition {
58	    /// Store this argon2id PHC string. The account can `createSession` with a password.
59	    Hashed(String),
60	    /// Store NULL. The account authenticates through the device-key paths (wallet-confirmed
61	    /// OAuth consent, sovereign sessions) and through app passwords for standard clients — the
62	    /// same column state migration-mode `createAccount` has always written for OAuth-only accounts.
63	    None,
64	}
65	
66	impl PasswordDisposition {
67	    /// The value to bind to `accounts.password_hash`.
68	    pub(crate) fn as_column(&self) -> Option<&str> {
69	        match self {
70	            Self::Hashed(hash) => Some(hash.as_str()),
71	            Self::None => None,
72	        }
73	    }
74	}
75	
76	/// Decide what an account is created with, given the password the client supplied (`None` when
77	/// the field was omitted entirely) and whether the operator allows passwordless accounts
78	/// (`accounts.password_optional`, advertised as the `optionalPassword` capability).
79	///
80	/// Returning `Err` refuses the request outright — nothing is written.
81	///
82	/// The empty string is deliberately not a way to ask for a passwordless account: `""` is what an
83	/// uninitialized form field serializes to, so honoring it would let a client bug silently produce
84	/// an account with no password. Omission is the unambiguous signal, and it is the only one
85	/// accepted — under either policy.
86	///
87	/// Shared by the two account-creation routes (`create_did`, `create_account_xrpc`), which cannot
88	/// import each other, so the policy cannot drift between the native ceremony and the standard
89	/// XRPC path.
90	pub(crate) fn resolve_password(
91	    supplied: Option<&str>,
92	    password_optional: bool,
93	) -> Result<PasswordDisposition, ApiError> {
94	    match supplied {
95	        // argon2 happily hashes "", so without this the PDS would store a zero-length password.
96	        // Refused under both policies: it is indistinguishable from an uninitialized field, and
97	        // guessing which of the two a client meant is a guess worth not making.
98	        Some("") => Err(ApiError::new(
99	            ErrorCode::InvalidClaim,
100	            "password must not be empty; omit the field entirely to create a passwordless account",
101	        )),
102	        Some(password) => Ok(PasswordDisposition::Hashed(hash_password(password)?)),
103	        None if password_optional => Ok(PasswordDisposition::None),
104	        // Named separately from the empty-string case: the client sent no password at all, and
105	        // telling it "must not be empty" would send it looking for a bug it does not have.
106	        None => Err(ApiError::new(
107	            ErrorCode::InvalidClaim,
108	            "password is required; this server does not offer passwordless accounts",
109	        )),
110	    }
111	}
112	
113	/// Verify `password` against a stored argon2id PHC-format hash string.
114	///
115	/// Returns `CorruptHash` if `stored_hash` cannot be parsed as a PHC string.
116	/// The caller is responsible for logging with the account identifier and returning a
117	/// 500 without incrementing the rate-limit counter — corrupt hash is a server-side
118	/// defect, not a user authentication failure.

120	    let Ok(hash) = PasswordHash::new(stored_hash) else {
121	        return VerifyResult::CorruptHash;
122	    };
123	    match Argon2::default().verify_password(password.as_bytes(), &hash) {
124	        Ok(()) => VerifyResult::Ok,
125	        Err(_) => VerifyResult::WrongPassword,
126	    }
127	}

## What landed

**Server** — `accounts.password_optional` (default `false`, `EZPDS_ACCOUNTS_PASSWORD_OPTIONAL`); `optionalPassword` in the capability table gated on exactly that flag; `resolve_password` + `PasswordDisposition` in [auth/password.rs](crates/pds/src/auth/password.rs), called by both `create_did` and `create_account_xrpc`.

**Wallet** — capability const/accessor, `Option<String>` password through the ceremony chain with `skip_serializing_if` so omission is real on the wire, capability captured at the `pds_config` probe and read at the handle step, `passwordless-signup` harness scenario.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- `resolve_password` had to go in `auth/password.rs`, not the route: the crate's hard rule is that routes never import routes, so the two creation paths could otherwise drift on what a password means. It's also genuinely Functional Core — config in, disposition out.
- The default harness fixture deliberately does *not* advertise the capability. Adding it there would have silently flipped every other scenario onto the passwordless path, including the ones the docs screenshots are generated from — the with-password flow is still what most hosts do, so it stays the default fixture.
- The `Option<String>` + `#[serde(default)]` shape is what creates the omitted-vs-empty distinction at all. As a plain `String`, serde collapses "absent" into an error and `""` into a value, so the policy you chose would have had nothing to act on.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

## Verification

- `pds` + `common`: **2231 + 196 pass**, 0 fail (baseline on main was 2226, so +5 new)
- iOS cross-compile of the wallet: clean
- `pnpm check`: 442 files, 0 errors · `pnpm test`: 171 pass
- clippy `-D warnings`: clean · `ticket-ref-check`, `capability-docs-check`, `bruno-check`, `changelog-check`, `docs-check`: all pass
- Browser harness: the A/B above

Two things worth knowing. First, an intermediate full-suite run showed six unrelated failures (`get_blob`, `didweb_migration`); they passed in isolation, the unmodified main checkout passed 2226/2226, and the next worktree run passed 2231/2231 — transient, and the disk is at **99% (6.7 GiB free)**, which is the likely cause and will bite other work. Second, an early `cargo check` reported success against the *main* checkout because `nix develop` runs from the workspace root; every result above uses an explicit `--manifest-path` into the worktree.

Not done, deliberately: `just ci` end-to-end (`cargo fmt --all` breaks in this worktree via the vendored plugin crates, so I rustfmt'd the touched files directly and ran the other gates individually), and `cargo audit`/`deny`, which no dependency change here can affect.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/jacob.zweifel/.claude/skills/linear-workflow

# Linear Development Workflow

This skill manages the full lifecycle of working on a Linear issue: from picking it up through opening a PR.

## Starting Work on an Issue

When the user indicates they want to work on a Linear issue (e.g., "Let's work on MM-42"):

1. **Parse the issue identifier** from the user's message. The pattern is `MM-` followed by a number.

2. **Fetch the issue details** from Linear using the `get_issue` tool with the parsed identifier. Display a brief summary to the user: title, description (truncated if long), priority, and any existing labels.

3. **Update the issue in Linear:**
   - Set the status to **"In Progress"**
   - Assign it to **"me"** (the authenticated user)

   Use the `save_issue` tool with the issue's `id`, `state: "In Progress"`, and `assignee: "me"`.

4. **Create a git branch from a fresh base** using the issue's suggested branch name:
   - The `get_issue` response includes a `branchName` field — use that as the branch name.
   - **Fetch first, then branch from the remote tip — never from a possibly-stale local HEAD:**
     `git fetch origin main && git checkout -b <branchName> origin/main`
     A stale base silently duplicates work that already merged (hours lost rebuilding an already-shipped backend is the known failure mode).
   - If the branch already exists locally, check it out, then run `git log --oneline <branchName>..origin/main` and surface to the user how far behind the base is.

5. **Verify sibling work is in the base.** If the issue depends on or overlaps sibling issues already marked Done in Linear, confirm their PRs are actually present in the branch base (e.g. `git log --oneline origin/main | grep -i mm-nnn`, or check for the files/routes they added) before concluding any related feature is "missing". **"Linear says Done but the code isn't here" is a hard stop-and-verify signal — it almost always means your base is stale, not that the feature needs building.**

6. **Confirm to the user** what happened: issue assigned, status updated, branch created/checked out (and from which base commit). Then ask what they'd like to tackle first, or summarize the issue so they can dive in.

## Opening a PR (Auto-transition to "In Review")

When the user asks to open a PR, create a pull request, or you detect that a PR is being created for a branch associated with a Linear issue:

1. **Identify the Linear issue** from the current branch name. Linear branch names typically contain the issue identifier (e.g., `malpercio/mm-42-fix-the-thing`). Extract the `MM-XXX` portion.

2. **Create the PR** as the user requests (follow normal PR creation workflow).

3. **After the PR is successfully created**, update the Linear issue:
   - Set the status to **"In Review"**
   - Attach the PR URL as a link on the issue using the `links` field in `save_issue`

   Use `save_issue` with the issue's `id`, `state: "In Review"`, and `links: [{"url": "<pr-url>", "title": "Pull Request"}]`.

4. **Confirm** to the user that the issue has been moved to "In Review" and the PR link has been attached.

## Important Notes

- Always fetch the issue first to confirm it exists and get the full `id` (UUID) needed for updates.
- If the issue is already "In Progress" and assigned, skip those updates and just create the branch.
- If branch creation fails (e.g., uncommitted changes), inform the user and suggest next steps rather than silently failing.
- The PR-to-"In Review" transition should happen automatically whenever a PR is opened during a session where the user started work on a Linear issue. Track the active issue identifier throughout the session.

content.text: All expected. Committing:

input.command:
cd "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)" && git add -A && git commit -F - <<'EOF'
Operator-gated optional password at account creation (MM-481)

Adds `accounts.password_optional` (default false,
`EZPDS_ACCOUNTS_PASSWORD_OPTIONAL`) and advertises it as a new
`optionalPassword` capability. With it on, a client may omit the password
field when creating an account; the account stores a NULL `password_hash`
and authenticates through its device key — wallet-confirmed OAuth consent
and sovereign sessions — plus app passwords for standard ATProto clients.

This is requirement-removal only. `accounts.password_hash` has been
nullable since V008 and migration-mode `createAccount` has always stored
NULL, so the schema was already passwordless-ready; only the input
validation in `/v1/dids` and `createAccount`'s new-account mode was not.
Existing passworded accounts are untouched, and the flag is off by
default: a passwordless account depends on device-key custody an operator
cannot verify on the account holder's behalf.

An empty-string password is refused under either policy. `""` is what an
uninitialized form field serializes to, so honoring it would let a client
bug silently create an account with no credential — omission is the only
way to ask, and the two rejections carry distinct messages so a client is
not sent looking for a bug it does not have.

The policy lives in `auth::password::resolve_password` rather than in
either route, since routes cannot import each other and the native
ceremony and the standard XRPC path must not drift on what a password
means.

Wallet: reads the capability from the probe `PdsConfigScreen` already
performs and skips the password screen entirely against a host that
advertises it, while still collecting one everywhere else — including a
host that could not be reached, which is the safe direction. The three
account-creation error branches that recovered to the password step now
fall back to the handle step when that step does not exist, so a failed
passwordless signup cannot strand the user on a screen the flow omits.

Does not ship to a public beta before MM-480 (in-wallet create-flow
consent): a passwordless account cannot yet complete its own signup,
because the post-create consent page offers only a password form and a
wallet handoff pointing back at the app hosting the takeover. MM-479
(deleteAccount rework) is the other prerequisite — a passwordless account
currently cannot be deleted.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF

cd "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)" && gh pr create --base main --title "Operator-gated optional password at account creation (MM-481)" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
Adds an operator switch that lets accounts be created with no password at all, advertised as a new `optionalPassword` capability, and teaches the wallet to skip its password screen against a host that offers it.

First half of Phase 1 of [`docs/design-plans/2026-07-12-passwordless-auth.md`](docs/design-plans/2026-07-12-passwordless-auth.md). Tracked as [MM-481](https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-481/operator-gated-optional-password-at-account-creation-optionalpassword).

## Why

`accounts.password_hash` has been nullable since V008 and migration-mode `createAccount` has always stored NULL, so the schema was already passwordless-ready — only the input validation in `/v1/dids` and `createAccount`'s new-account mode was not. This is **requirement**-removal, not support-removal: existing passworded accounts are untouched, and nothing changes unless an operator opts in.

Off by default, because a passwordless account depends on device-key custody an operator cannot verify on the account holder's behalf. A deployment whose users are not all running the wallet should keep the password required.

## Shape

**Server**

- `accounts.password_optional` on the existing `AccountsConfig` (default `false`, `EZPDS_ACCOUNTS_PASSWORD_OPTIONAL`).
- New `optionalPassword` entry in the capability table, gated on exactly that flag — `capabilities.rs` requires the advertised condition to be the one the routes actually enforce, so the predicate is the config field itself.
- `auth::password::resolve_password` decides the account's password disposition before any state is written. It lives in `auth/` rather than either route because routes cannot import each other, and the native ceremony and the standard XRPC path must not drift on what a password means.

**An empty-string password is refused under either policy.** `""` is what an uninitialised form field serializes to, so honouring it would let a client bug silently mint an account with no credential. Omission is the only way to ask — and the two rejections carry distinct messages, so a client that sent nothing is not told to go looking for an empty field it never had.

**Wallet**

- Reads the capability from the probe `PdsConfigScreen` already performs (no extra round trip) and skips `PasswordScreen` entirely when the host advertises it.
- Still collects a password everywhere else — including against a host that could not be reached, which is the safe direction: a password sent to a host that would have allowed omitting it still creates a working account, whereas the reverse fails the ceremony outright. An older Custos deployment is unaffected, which matters because the TestFlight build and the prod deploy do not update in lockstep.
- The three account-creation error branches that recovered to `step = 'password'` now fall back to `handle` when that step does not exist, so a failed passwordless signup cannot strand the user on a screen the flow omits.
- `password` travels as `Option<String>` with `skip_serializing_if`, so omission is a genuinely absent field on the wire rather than a `null` or an empty string.

## Not shipping to a public beta yet

Two prerequisites, both filed and both discovered while building this:

- **[MM-480](https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-480/create-flow-approve-oauth-consent-in-wallet-without-a-browser-takeover)** — a passwordless account cannot currently complete its own signup. The post-create OAuth consent page offers a password form (unusable) and a wallet handoff that points at the app hosting the takeover (unreachable). Fixing it by hiding the password form for accounts that lack one is *not* safe: `oauth_authorize.rs` deliberately leaves `account_did` NULL because `login_hint` is unverified, so branching the page on whether an account has a password would make `GET /oauth/authorize` an unauthenticated account-existence oracle.
- **[MM-479](https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-479/passwordless-accounts-rework-deleteaccount-to-email-token-or-wallet)** — a passwordless account cannot be deleted. `delete_account.rs` folds "no password on file" into the generic credential failure and returns 401.

The flag is safe to merge ahead of both (it is off by default and this is an n=1 deployment); it is not safe to *enable* ahead of them.

## Verification

- `pds` **2231 pass** / `common` **196 pass**, 0 failures (baseline on `main` was 2226 — five new tests: the three-way policy matrix, the passwordless end-to-end ceremony asserting NULL `password_hash`, and empty-string refusal with the flag on).
- One pre-existing test changed contract deliberately: an omitted password used to be a 422 from the deserializer and is now a 400 from the policy, which is what lets the response say *why*.
- `cargo clippy --all-targets -D warnings` clean; iOS cross-compile of the wallet clean.
- `pnpm check` 452 files 0 errors; `pnpm test` 191 pass.
- `ticket-ref-check`, `capability-docs-check`, `bruno-check`, `changelog-check`, `docs-check` all pass.
- Driven end to end in the browser harness, both directions: with `optionalPassword` advertised the handle step goes straight to the sealing ceremony; without it, the same flow lands on "Create a password". A `passwordless-signup` scenario was added for this — deliberately *not* by adding the capability to the default fixture, which would have silently flipped every other scenario and the docs screenshots onto the passwordless path.

## Dependencies

None added.

EOF

# Batch PR Review-Comment Triage

Pull every unresolved review thread on the current PR in one command, then triage the batch. The user should never have to paste review comments one at a time.

## Fetch unresolved threads

Determine the PR number for the current branch (`gh pr view --json number -q .number`), then:

```bash
gh api graphql -f query='
query($owner:String!,$repo:String!,$pr:Int!){
  repository(owner:$owner,name:$repo){
    pullRequest(number:$pr){
      reviewThreads(first:100){
        nodes{
          isResolved isOutdated path line
          comments(first:30){nodes{author{login} body url}}
```

2. **Legitimate but out of scope** — file a follow-up issue rather than growing the PR.
3. **Pure style nit / preference** — decline with a one-line reason.

Present the full disposition table (thread → classification → action) to the user in ONE message before applying fixes, so they approve the batch rather than each item. Note that every fix-commit re-triggers CI and (for assertive bots like CodeRabbit) a fresh review round that tends to find one more micro-nit — batch fixes into a single commit where possible.

toolUseResult.originalFile: Operators can now let accounts be created without a password at all. With `[accounts] password_optional = true` (`EZPDS_ACCOUNTS_PASSWORD_OPTIONAL`) the server advertises a new `optionalPassword` capability, and a client may omit the password field when creating an account; the account then authenticates through its device key — wallet-confirmed OAuth consent and sovereign sessions — plus app passwords for standard AT Protocol clients. The identity wallet reads that capability and skips its password screen entirely against such a host, while continuing to ask for one everywhere else, so an older deployment is unaffected. Off by default: a passwordless account depends on device-key custody an operator cannot verify for the account holder. An empty password is rejected either way — an empty string is what an uninitialised form field sends, so omitting the field is the only way to ask for a passwordless account.

content.text:
Handled — [PR #462](https://github.com/malpercio-dev/ezpds/pull/462) updated, all four CodeRabbit threads resolved.

## One finding was real, and it was mine

CodeRabbit rated it "Trivial / nitpick"; it was a genuine regression. Folding the argon2 hash into `resolve_password` moved it to the front of both creation routes. On `main`, `create_account_xrpc.rs` checked password *presence* cheaply at L113 and hashed at L234 — after `validate_handle` and genesis-op verification. My version made an unauthenticated endpoint, bounded only by a per-IP rate limit, pay a deliberately-slow hash before failing on free local checks.

I took a different fix than proposed. Moving the whole call later restores the late hash but loses the early rejection. Splitting them keeps both: `resolve_password` returns a `PasswordPlan` and hashes nothing; `PasswordPlan::hash()` runs at each route's original hash point.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
This is a nice illustration of why "extract the shared logic" isn't free. Pulling both routes' password handling into one function looked like pure deduplication — but the two halves had *different scheduling requirements*: the policy check wanted to be early, the hash wanted to be late. Merging them silently picked one schedule for both. The borrowed-`&str` plan type is what lets the shared decision travel to the call site that knows when to spend the CPU.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

## Three declined, with reasons posted

- **Biometric gate before passwordless signing** (flagged Major/Security) — wrong premise. This screen has never had a biometric gate, on `main` or here; both paths are gated by press-and-hold. The guideline it cites covers signing against an *existing* identity, where the device key already carries authority. Here the key is being minted.
- **"afterward" / "in both modes"** — the claimed "project's American-English wording" isn't a convention this repo has: `afterwards` 7 vs `afterward` 4, `initialised` 2 vs `initialized` 1. That's LanguageTool's default locale. Offered to adopt a repo-wide rule as a separate linted sweep.
- **CodeQL "hard-coded cryptographic value" ×2** — test passwords in `#[cfg(test)]`. Skipped silently per your standing directive on GHAS threads; no comment posted.

**Accepted:** the changelog now says "Obsign" rather than "the identity wallet", per the release-facing convention.

## Re-verified after the change

`pds` **2231** / `common` **196** pass · clippy `-D warnings` clean · all five drift gates pass. The two tests CodeRabbit warned were order-dependent needed no edit — the policy check kept its position, only the hashing moved.

Commit `a7e93392`. Expect one more CodeRabbit round on the new commit; I'll leave it unless something lands.

cd "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)" && nix develop --impure --accept-flake-config -c rustfmt --edition 2021 apps/identity-wallet/src-tauri/src/lib.rs 2>/dev/null; git add -A && git commit -F - <<'EOF'
Fix the wallet's CreateDidRequest tests for the optional password (MM-481)

The iOS PR gate compiles the wallet's test target; two `CreateDidRequest`
serialization tests still built `password` from a `&str`, which stopped
coercing when the field became `Option<String>`.

My local check was `cargo build --lib --target aarch64-apple-ios`, which
compiles the library but not `#[cfg(test)]`, so it passed while CI's
`--all-targets` did not.

Also adds the test that was missing: a passwordless request must omit
`password` from the wire entirely — not `null`, not `""`. That is the
contract `skip_serializing_if` exists for, and nothing else on the wallet
side would have caught its removal.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
git push 2>&1 | tail -3
